proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(a=1-\alpha\).  Because \(\alpha\in(0,1/4)\), one has \(a\in(3/4,1)\).  Fix an index \(n\) for which \(\kappa_n\le 1/16\).  By \(\text{thm:integrated-and-bump-lower-frontier}\),
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\ge G_\alpha(\tau_n).
\]
By \(\text{def:integrated-slope-lower-function}\),
\[
 G_\alpha(\tau_n)
 =2\int_0^1 [a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t}]_+\,dt.
\]
For every \(t\in[0,1]\), \(\sqrt{\tau_n t}\le \sqrt{\tau_n}\).  Since \(x\mapsto[x]_+\) is nondecreasing,
\[
 [a-4\sqrt{\tau_n t}]_+
 \ge [a-4\sqrt{\tau_n}]_+.
\]
Integration over \([0,1]\) therefore gives
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)
 \ge G_\alpha(\tau_n)
 \ge 2[a-4\sqrt{\tau_n}]_+
 =2[1-\alpha-4\sqrt{\tau_n}]_+.
\]

For the upper bound, define the measurable sample rule
\[
 I_n^0(O_1,\ldots,O_n)
 =
 \begin{cases}
   \Theta,& X_1\le 1-\alpha,\\
   \{0\},& X_1>1-\alpha.
 \end{cases}
\]
Its two possible values are connected subsets of \(\Theta=[-1,1]\), and their lengths are respectively \(2\) and \(0\).  For every \(P\in\mathcal P_n\), the definition of \(\Theta\) gives \(\theta_P\in\Theta\).  Hence, using \(\text{ass:uniform-running-variable}\),
\[
 P\{\theta_P\in I_n^0(O_1,\ldots,O_n)\}
 \ge P\{X_1\le 1-\alpha\}
 =1-\alpha.
\]
Thus \(I_n^0\) satisfies the uniform honesty constraint in \(\text{def:minimax-length}\).  The same assumption yields, for every \(P\in\mathcal P_n\),
\[
 E_P\bigl[|I_n^0(O_1,\ldots,O_n)|\bigr]
 =2P\{X_1\le1-\alpha\}
 =2(1-\alpha).
\]
Taking this single data-driven rule as a competitor in the infimum defining \(L_n^\star\) proves
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\le2(1-\alpha).
\]

Now suppose \(\tau_n\to0\).  Since \(n\ge1\) and \(\tau_n=n\kappa_n^3\), one has \(0<\kappa_n^3\le\tau_n\), and hence \(\kappa_n\to0\).  Thus \(\kappa_n\le1/16\) eventually, so the two preceding bounds apply eventually.  Their lower endpoint converges to \(2(1-\alpha)\), while their upper endpoint equals \(2(1-\alpha)\).  The squeeze theorem gives
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\longrightarrow2(1-\alpha).
\]

Finally, fix \(s>1\) and suppose that \(\lambda_n\) remains in a compact subset of \((0,\infty)\).  In particular, \(\lambda_n\) is bounded above.  We first prove \(\kappa_n\to0\).  Otherwise there are \(\epsilon>0\) and a subsequence, still denoted by \(n\), such that \(\kappa_n\ge\epsilon\).  The global strength range \(\kappa_n\le1/8\) ensures \(0<\epsilon\le1/8\).  Since \(x\mapsto\log(e/x)\) is decreasing on \((0,\infty)\), the definition of \(\lambda_n\) implies along this subsequence
\[
 \lambda_n
 =\frac{n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}}{\log(e/\kappa_n)}
 \ge
 \frac{n\epsilon^{2+1/s}}{\log(e/\epsilon)}
 \longrightarrow\infty,
\]
contradicting boundedness.  Therefore \(\kappa_n\to0\), so in particular \(\kappa_n\le1/16\) eventually.  From the defining identity
\[
 \lambda_n
 =\frac{\tau_n\kappa_n^{1/s-1}}{\log(e/\kappa_n)}
\]
we obtain
\[
 \tau_n
 =\lambda_n\kappa_n^{1-1/s}\log(e/\kappa_n).
\]
Here \(1-1/s>0\).  The elementary limit \(x^{1-1/s}\log(e/x)\to0\) as \(x\downarrow0\), together with the upper boundedness of \(\lambda_n\), therefore gives \(\tau_n\to0\).  Applying the preceding squeeze on the eventual range \(\kappa_n\le1/16\) proves
\[
 L_n^\star(\kappa_n)\longrightarrow2(1-\alpha),
\]
as claimed.
